name: Daria Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal shift at the housing-repairs contact centre?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the team that gets the leaking ceilings after the routine booking script has failed. I check the tenant's photo, the repair history and whether somebody can safely stay in the room tonight. I use AI every day to sort the queue and draft updates, then I call the contractor and check the decision myself. My two-year college diploma helped with the rules, but the urgent calls taught me how to hear panic under a calm voice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your household count on from that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leila supervises a school kitchen, and our grown children pay their own bills elsewhere. My lead shifts bring higher pay than the usual agent rate. We rent, and we have about thirteen months of expenses saved. That lets us make a careful choice, but Leila's kitchen wage alone would not keep our whole flat and its bills going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues the queue sorter is useful when it puts a burst pipe above a loose cupboard door. I still want a person to check the photo and tell the tenant which contractor is really coming. A better draft message doesn't fix a wet ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid lead rota should continue, and Leila's kitchen should too. Thirteen months saved means a repair or a gap would not empty us immediately. I use AI daily now, but I don't ask it to decide whether a family can sleep beside a leak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep the paid repairs queue, check AI sorting against the photos and contractor record, and call tenants back with an actual visit time. If the plateau continues into its first year, I'll keep those same checks and our ordinary rent payments from wages. I won't count a quicker message as a new source of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. There is room to do the job carefully and both wages look steady. The repair booking is only finished when the tenant knows who is coming through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake does a queue sorter make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A photo of a dark ceiling can be a fresh leak or an old stain, and a tool may not know which room a child sleeps in. I ring the tenant if the record and picture disagree. The contractor needs a real address, not an elegant sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own housing costs. Leila and I can use the reserve for a real gap and keep paying ordinary rent from wages. Thirteen months saved is good protection, not a reason to hand our children a bill.

say: I'd keep **urgent repair photos** and contractor times checked by a person.
I'd call a **faster message** helpful only when the actual visit is confirmed.
think: I expect the **paid lead rota** and Leila's kitchen work to continue.
I use AI **daily already**, without giving it the safety decision.
do: Keep the **paid repairs queue** and compare AI sorting with photos and contractor records.
Call **tenants back** with confirmed visit times while rent stays paid from current wages.
feel: **Calm** about both wages and the ability to make careful repair decisions.
S0.quote: The repair booking is only finished when the tenant knows who is coming through the door.
fieldNote: Daily **AI sorting and drafting** are existing work habits, so this mild scenario creates no new AI-learning action.
Her **higher lead pay** and thirteen-month reserve protect ordinary uncertainty without relying on grown children's wages.

steps.text: Keep paid housing-repair calls and check AI sorting against photos and contractor records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team automated booking may take the simple jobs, but a person must still be able to dispatch help when a ceiling is wet. I would join our union branch in asking for a paid urgent-appeal rota with that authority. The landlord should publish changes in paid shifts, not hide them behind a nicer dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead judgement may still be needed, but the team could lose paid hours as the easy calls go. The new photo-risk verifier is not the queue sorter I already use. I want to test it against real repairs before trusting it on a tenant's ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll join colleagues' written request for paid urgent-appeal shifts with dispatch authority and cut dates. If the employer gives us paid time with real closed cases and the verifier catches a leak the old queue missed, I'll learn it by comparing its ratings with technician visits and recording missed emergencies. I'll keep handling paid escalations while the rota remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the paid week, though I can test something real. An AI system can label a leak minor; a wet ceiling cannot read that label. If the verifier misses a serious case, a person needs power to change the dispatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the verifier worth learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check a week's photos against what the technicians found, not just the colour of a dashboard score. If it catches a leak the old queue missed, I'll learn the tool on paid time. If it hides a leak, I'll put that case in the shared error log before anybody relies on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would join the request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agents who take urgent calls, the union delegate and the repair schedulers who see the consequences. We would ask for paid shifts and the right to change a dispatch, not a meeting to admire software. I'd sign the request with the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila that full thinking AI by 2028 could handle repair calls before our team finishes breakfast. Robots entering flats come around 2031, which does not save a desk job. I'd ask the union to demand notice and a paid person who can order urgent human repairs when an AI decision is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead rota could end with the rest of the queue. Thirteen months of savings buys a search, not a paid organiser's post. Leila's kitchen wage cannot cover our rent and essentials alone, and I won't write our grown children's wages into the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll join the union group's written demand for closure dates and paid urgent-repair appeals, and keep my paid calls while the rota exists. If the repair line ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for a posted paid union field-organiser role only if its written weekly hours and after-travel wage, together with Leila's actual pay, cover our rent and essential bills. I will start field visits only after a signed paid offer and a safe travel plan for evening meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a lead income disappearing quickly, even with money saved. I can arrange a meeting and hear a grievance; I cannot make a union advertise a paid organiser job. I'd rather keep searching than pretend an unpaid committee seat replaces rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would field organising involve for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going to workplaces, hearing workers' cases and asking the employer to correct a decision in front of the people affected. I would want paid hours and safe routes home after evening meetings. An AI can draft a demand, but a worker still needs somebody who will stand beside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid organiser opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd search other posted local paid work against our written rent budget while using only a bounded part of the existing reserve. If any call shifts still pay, I keep them until the line actually ends. I won't count volunteer union work or our children's wages as income.

say: I'd join a **union notice demand** and seek paid urgent-repair appeals.
I'd tell Leila **2028 AGI** reaches calls before 2031 indoor robots.
think: I expect the **lead rota** could end quickly.
I know thirteen months saved and Leila's wage cannot cover **rent and essentials** indefinitely.
do: Join the **union group demand** for written closure dates and paid urgent-repair appeals in 2026.
After line closure, apply for **posted paid field organising** only if written weekly hours and after-travel household pay cover rent/essentials.
Keep **paid calls**; start visits after closure, signed offer and safe travel; without post, seek budgeted posted paid work with bounded reserve.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of higher pay despite a thirteen-month reserve.
S2.quote: Thirteen months of savings buys a search, not a paid organiser's post.
fieldNote: Her **union demand** protects paid urgent-repair correction for tenants, separate from her possible paid organiser application.
An organiser application follows **actual line closure** and requires posted paid work with written weekly after-travel household rent coverage.
She refuses to count **volunteer work** or adult children's wages; safe evening travel and a signed offer gate field visits.

steps.text: Join union demand for written closure dates and paid urgent-repair appeal workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us build evidence from wrong repair decisions and ask for paid tenant appeals before full AGI reaches the phones in 2031. Robots around 2034 may handle physical repairs, but tenants still need a place to challenge unsafe decisions. I would not call a union badge a wage unless there is a paid post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can try real field casework while my higher paid lead shifts continue. The union may need a person in the room, but it might not have a vacancy. I could also lose my current team by 2031, so I want a measured route rather than a slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the union whether a posted paid field-organiser opening offers a paid observation day, and take it if offered to check meeting duties and safe travel home. I'll keep paid repair calls and help colleagues build a shared record of wrongly closed urgent cases. In the first year after 2031, if my lead hours are cut, I'll apply for a still-posted paid organiser job only if its written weekly hours and after-travel household wage with Leila's actual pay cover rent and essentials; I'll leave only after signing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer warning lets me find out whether paid field work exists. A grievance meeting is work only when somebody pays for the hours and lets me correct a decision. A title on a volunteer committee would not keep our flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shared error record be used for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The staff group would take actual missed leaks and dates to the operator and demand a paid appeal rota with authority to send a repairer. I would not publish tenants' addresses. This is a shared demand, not my private presentation about a clever tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid union job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep whatever paid lead calls remain and search other posted local paid work against our rent budget. We can use a bounded slice of the existing reserve while searching, but not treat it as monthly earnings. I would not leave a paid shift for a volunteer badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children that a decade helps us plan with statements, not make them our retirement fund. I will be sixty-eight in 2036, and I may still need paid work. Thinking AI reaches the repair calls then; robots about 2039 are a later issue for hands-on tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen months saved today is strong but not a lifetime wage, and Leila's kitchen pay can change. I would like to choose fewer shifts by then if our real income allows it. I won't assume any pension entitlement or a family rescue because the calendar says I am older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 Leila and I will review rent, savings and actual income every year, and I will keep paid housing-repair shifts while they are offered. I'll keep joining the staff group's request for paid urgent-appeal authority and protect the shared error record. In the first year after 2036, if AGI ends my paid calls and verified household income cannot cover rent and essentials, I'll seek posted paid local work; if our documented resources cover years of bills, I can decide whether to stop working without counting the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not certain. A decade lets us see what we can actually afford, but it does not write a wage on the page. I would rather make a gradual decision than have a machine's date pick it for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make fewer shifts possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Statements showing continuing income and savings covering rent, food, travel and repairs for years without my lead wage. I would not use a guessed pension figure or promise from our children. If the sums are short, I keep earning if paid work exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a tenant about appeals then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a tenant needs a paid person who can reopen an unsafe repair decision, even if I no longer answer the phone. I would still sign a group request for that right. A tenant needs a door that opens, not a ticket that closes.

fieldNote: She avoids assuming **pension rights** or financial help from grown children despite strong savings today.
The **staff group demand** remains paid repair-correction authority, backed by confidential error records.
A yearly **rent-and-income review** gates any reduced hours or exit; paid work remains necessary if bills are uncovered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the repair line and my lead pay could disappear before I have another paid role. Written closure dates, a paid urgent-appeal worker who can dispatch help, and a real organiser vacancy would help. A tenant needs a door that opens, not a ticket that closes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose address gets copied into a shared error file. We can demand fair repair decisions without publishing a tenant's bedroom photo. The union should have evidence and the tenant should keep privacy.

headlineQuote: The union should have evidence and the tenant should keep privacy.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Daria leads urgent housing-repair calls using a two-year diploma and daily AI sorting that she checks against real safety needs.
She has **higher lead pay**, thirteen months saved, rent, a partner on school-kitchen wages and independent grown children.
She learns a **new AI photo verifier** only through paid real-case comparison and joins a staff demand for dispatch-correction authority.
Fast AGI threatens the **whole repair queue**; longer warnings let her test paid field organising without counting volunteer work as income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end the repair line and her higher lead pay before another paid role is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Written closure dates**, paid urgent-repair appeals with dispatch power and a real paid organiser vacancy would help.
